title: Filter Far More, Take Most Back

scenes.tts: In an adult human, the kidneys filter about one hundred and eighty litres of plasma a day. That is about four times the water in the whole body. Yet most people pass only one or two litres of urine. Where does the rest go? Back into the blood.
scenes.caption: In an adult human, the kidneys filter about 180 litres of plasma a day. That is about four times the water in the whole body. Yet most people pass only one or two litres of urine. Where does the rest go? Back into the blood.
scenes.visual: Tall blue bar of filtered plasma against a sliver of urine, red question mark; the bar moves into a blood box and leaves only the sliver.
scenes.narration: In an adult human, the kidneys filter about 180 litres of plasma a day. That is about four times the water in the whole body. Yet most people pass only one or two litres of urine. Where does the rest go? Back into the blood.

scenes.tts: The working unit is the nephron: a filter attached to a long tube. In mammals, the afferent arteriole carries blood into the glomerulus, a knot of capillaries. The efferent arteriole carries it out. Afferent in, efferent out. Blood pressure pushes plasma through a barrier into Bowman's capsule. The filtrate holds water and small solutes, but no blood cells, and very little protein.
scenes.visual: Afferent arrow into a glomerulus box inside a capsule; efferent arrow out to peritubular capillaries; filtrate arrows into a tube; chips for what passes.
scenes.narration: The working unit is the nephron: a filter attached to a long tube. In mammals, the afferent arteriole carries blood into the glomerulus, a knot of capillaries. The efferent arteriole carries it out. Afferent in, efferent out. Blood pressure pushes plasma through a barrier into Bowman's capsule. The filtrate holds water and small solutes, but no blood cells, and very little protein.

scenes.tts: The filtrate flows on through the proximal tubule, the loop of Henle, the distal tubule and the collecting duct. In mammals, the proximal tubule reabsorbs, or takes back into the blood, about sixty to seventy percent of filtered sodium. Water follows. It also takes back almost all the filtered glucose and amino acids.

scenes.visual: A dot travels the labelled nephron tube in order; arrows carry sodium, water, glucose and amino acids from the proximal tube to a blood bar.

scenes.tts: Now the loop of Henle, a hairpin with two lanes. The thick ascending limb moves sodium chloride out of the tube. It is nearly impermeable to water. Salt leaves, water stays, and the tissue outside gets saltier. The thin descending limb is permeable to water, at least in the rabbit. Water leaves it by osmosis. Because the lanes run in opposite directions, a modest difference adds up. In rat kidney slices, osmolality rises from the cortex to the papilla.
scenes.visual: Loop highlighted; salt arrows leave the thick ascending limb, a blocked water arrow, tissue shading grows saltier downward; water arrows leave the descending limb; arrow marks osmolality rising cortex to papilla.
scenes.narration: Now the loop of Henle, a hairpin with two lanes. The thick ascending limb moves sodium chloride out of the tube. It is nearly impermeable to water. Salt leaves, water stays, and the tissue outside gets saltier. The thin descending limb is permeable to water, at least in the rabbit. Water leaves it by osmosis. Because the lanes run in opposite directions, a modest difference adds up. In rat kidney slices, osmolality rises from the cortex to the papilla.

scenes.tts: The collecting duct runs through that salty tissue. With antidiuretic hormone, called A D H, its cells insert stored water channels into the membrane facing the urine. Water leaves by osmosis, and the urine becomes concentrated. Without A D H, the duct stays nearly water-tight, and dilute urine flows out. A water-deprived adult human can make urine near twelve hundred milliosmoles per kilogram. Plasma is about two hundred and ninety.
scenes.caption: The collecting duct runs through that salty tissue. With antidiuretic hormone, called ADH, its cells insert stored water channels into the membrane facing the urine. Water leaves by osmosis, and the urine becomes concentrated. Without ADH, the duct stays nearly water-tight, and dilute urine flows out. A water-deprived adult human can make urine near 1,200 mOsm/kg. Plasma is about 290.
scenes.visual: Duct in salty tissue: with ADH orange channels open and water leaves; reset; without ADH no channels, dilute urine; then two bars, plasma 290 and urine 1,200 mOsm/kg.

scenes.tts: Three verbs describe one nephron. Filtration pushes fluid out of the blood into the tube. Reabsorption moves substances back into the blood. Secretion moves substances from the blood into the tube. In mammals, the collecting duct sets the final water and salt content of urine. The kidney filters far more than it lets go.
